title: When Do Gaussian Priors Fail? A Latent Geometry Investigation of RL Fine-Tuning

paper.title:
When Do Gaussian Priors Fail? A Latent Geometry
Investigation of RL Fine-Tuning
paper.abstract:
Abstract Latent diffusion models almost universally place a Gaussian prior 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) on the VAE latent space. For base generation this
default is unproblematic; under reinforcement-learning fine-tuning,
however, it carries a structural limitation. We show that the standard
VAE’s KL term does not merely ignore mode structure — it actively
taxes separation and tightness. When the data are multimodal, the ELBO
optimum therefore compresses distinct modes into an overlapping latent
envelope. RL fine-tuning amplifies this overlap: the score network is
under-resolved on the saddle region between modes, the
dynamic-to-variational error amplification rises sharply, and the
collapse boundary β c \beta_{c} — the minimum KL strength that preserves
mode coverage — is pushed far above its variational scale. The effect
is large and reproducible: on the real alanine-dipeptide Boltzmann
distribution, a Gaussian-prior VAE collapses at β c = 0.224 \beta_{c}=0.224 , while
a mode-tracked Gaussian-mixture prior on the same data collapses at 3.16 × 10 − 3 3.16\times 10^{-3} — a 71 × 71\times gap produced by the same pipeline. We trace this gap to a single geometric mediator, d min / ( 2 ​ σ 0 ) d_{\min}/(2\sigma_{0}) , and verify the causal chain through controlled
interventions: moving geometry at fixed prior, and switching prior at
matched geometry (full mediation; prior-label coefficient 0.995 × 0.995\times ,
95% CI [ 0.79 , 1.25 ] [0.79,1.25] ). A three-source decomposition localises the
amplification to the learned policy (zero ODE-solver contribution,
bounded and non-systematic anchor mismatch); the coverage plateau, by
contrast, is an unconditional benefit of mode-separating priors that no
amount of RL capacity recovers. We state the remedy conditionally: a
non-Gaussian prior is necessary precisely when the latent geometry
would fall into the overlap regime and the downstream task is
coverage-sensitive. A machine-checked theory skeleton (Lean 4)
supports the KL pricing structure — a divergent compactness tax under
a Gaussian prior versus a finite assignment fee under a mixture — and
the position-versus-plateau distinction delimits what is finite-resource
from what requires changing the prior.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models are now the dominant paradigm in generative modelling: denoising diffusion probabilistic models ( Ho et al., 2020 ) and their score-based SDE generalisation ( Song et al., 2021 ) reach state-of-the-art sample quality through iterative denoising. Latent diffusion ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) made the paradigm scalable by running the diffusion process in the compressed latent space of a VAE ( Kingma and Welling, 2013 ) rather than in pixel space — the step that turned high-resolution and text-to-image synthesis into practical technology — and the latent-diffusion recipe now extends to video ( Blattmann et al., 2023 ) , while diffusion models more broadly have become standard tools in scientific design, from image scaffolds to de novo protein structure generation ( Watson et al., 2023 ) . In all of these deployed systems the VAE latent space carries a Gaussian prior 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) by default. A third layer is being installed on top of this stack: reinforcement-learning fine-tuning. DDPO ( Black et al., 2024 ) recasts denoising as a Markov decision process and maximises a downstream reward by policy gradient; DPOK ( Wallace et al., 2023 ) adds a KL regulariser anchoring the fine-tuned policy to the pretrained prior — the same alignment recipe that is mature on large language models ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) and is spreading rapidly across diffusion deployments. Latent diffusion pipelines thus almost universally place a Gaussian prior on the VAE latent space, and this default — unproblematic for base generation — carries a structural limitation that emerges precisely when the three layers above are combined: multimodal data, a tight VAE latent space, and RL fine-tuning. This paper asks when that limitation bites, why, and what to do about it. One clarification before the contribution: this is not yet another account of reward-overoptimisation. The RLHF literature already documents diversity loss from over-optimised rewards ( Gao et al., 2023 ; Lee et al., 2023 ) ; our concern is a different, upstream mechanism — the collapse boundary is set by prior geometry even when the reward is well designed and the KL strength is generous. The Gaussian prior issue is the precondition that determines where the boundary sits, not a pathology of the reward signal. Figure 1: Overview. (a) The data are multimodal: several separated modes in data space. (b) The VAE prior sets the latent separation-to-width ratio d min / ( 2 ​ σ 0 ) d_{\min}/(2\sigma_{0}) : under a Gaussian prior the modes can overlap, while a mixture prior keeps them separated. (c) Under KL-anchored RL fine-tuning, the collapse boundary β c \beta_{c} and the recovery plateau depend on that geometry (schematic; measured curves in §5).

sections.heading:
1. The limitation: a Gaussian prior packs multimodal data
into an overlapping latent.
sections.text: The KL term of the standard VAE objective pulls every encoder posterior toward the unit Gaussian, forcing σ lat ≈ 1 \sigma_{\mathrm{lat}}\approx 1 . When the data are multimodal, the encoder must therefore pack distinct modes into a single broad envelope: the latent modes overlap, and the separation-to-width ratio d min / ( 2 ​ σ 0 ) d_{\min}/(2\sigma_{0}) — the smallest inter-mode distance measured in units of the mode diameter — drops below 1 1 . This compression is not a training failure but the optimum of the Gaussian-ELBO objective itself: the KL term does not merely ignore mode structure — separation and tightness are exactly what it charges for (the KL pricing structure is quantified by Propositions 2 and 3 in § 3 ; Figure 2 shows the compression forming during training).

sections.heading:
2. When the limitation bites: RL fine-tuning amplifies
overlap.
sections.text: Overlap alone is not fatal: a base model still samples every mode from an overlapped latent. The damage appears when the frozen model is fine-tuned with a KL-anchored RL objective. Once d min / ( 2 ​ σ 0 ) < 1 d_{\min}/(2\sigma_{0})<1 , the score network is under-resolved on the saddle region between modes, the dynamic-to-variational amplification dyn / var \mathrm{dyn}/\mathrm{var} rises sharply, and fine-tuning piles mass onto the reward-target mode, pushing the collapse boundary β c \beta_{c} — the minimum KL strength that preserves coverage — far above its variational scale. The effect is not subtle: on the real alanine-dipeptide Boltzmann distribution (Exp7), a Gaussian-prior VAE lands at d min / ( 2 ​ σ 0 ) = 0.81 d_{\min}/(2\sigma_{0})=0.81 and collapses at β c = 0.224 \beta_{c}=0.224 , while a mode-tracked Gaussian-mixture prior on the same data holds 1.03 1.03 and collapses only at 3.16 × 10 − 3 3.16\times 10^{-3} — a 71 × 71\times gap produced by the same score/ODE/fine-tune pipeline.

sections.heading: 3. When a non-Gaussian prior is needed.
sections.text: The answer is conditional, and the conditions are checkable before training: a non-Gaussian prior is needed when the latent geometry would fall into the overlap regime and the downstream task is coverage-sensitive. condition non-Gaussian prior needed? multimodal data + + tight latent dimension yes — Gaussian ELBO packs modes into overlap RL fine-tuning with a single-target reward yes — RL amplifies whatever overlap exists unimodal data, or a wide latent dimension no — the Gaussian prior suffices base generation only, no RL fine-tuning no — overlap does not hurt the base model Table 1: Decision rule for prior choice. The failure mode is joint: multimodality creates the overlap and RL fine-tuning amplifies it. Neither factor alone requires changing the prior.

sections.heading:
4. The remedy: a mode-preserving prior keeps the geometry
out of the amplifier’s reach.
sections.text: A Gaussian-mixture prior ( Dilokthanakul et al., 2016 ; Jiang et al., 2017 ; Tomczak and Welling, 2018 ; Lee et al., 2021 ) permits each component to remain tight ( σ lat ≪ 1 \sigma_{\mathrm{lat}}\ll 1 ), and the ELBO then pushes the encoder to preserve the data’s mode separation rather than average over it. The downstream chain follows immediately: separated geometry ( d min / ( 2 ​ σ 0 ) > 1 d_{\min}/(2\sigma_{0})>1 ) keeps dyn / var \mathrm{dyn}/\mathrm{var} small, which keeps β c \beta_{c} at its variational scale and the coverage plateau full — → 1.00 0.70\!\to\!1.00 in the controlled 1D comparison (Exp5A, K = 10 K{=}10 ), → 0.73 0.58\!\to\!0.73 decoded coverage in the crowded 2D pack (Exp6, K = 30 K{=}30 , 3-seed mean), and ≈ → 1.0 \approx 0.67\!\to\!1.0 latent coverage on alanine dipeptide (Exp7). The prior change is therefore not a cosmetic improvement but, in the overlap regime, a necessary one: the latent geometry is not independently tunable at fixed prior, so switching the prior is the only lever that moves the geometry out of the amplifier’s reach (Appendices G , K ). The remedy has an explicit boundary condition. At the exact reverse-KL optimum, with unlimited policy capacity and complete optimisation, the collapse boundary is set by geometry alone and the variational prediction already gives an order-1 prior gap in Exp7 ( 0.69 × 0.69\times , versus the measured 71 × 71\times ): nearly everything measured is the finite-resource pipeline’s amplification, which geometric separation sidesteps rather than repairs. Under the pipelines we study — a 2-layer score MLP, 1000 1000 guidance steps, 150 150 ODE steps — the advantage is real, reproducible over seeds and MD sampling length (20 ns and 60 ns give identical β c \beta_{c} for matched priors), and architecture-independent within the tested family ( K = 30 K{=}30 pack and the 2-layer score MLP); whether it persists with a much larger policy and much longer optimisation is a testable limit we state rather than conceal.

sections.heading:
The mechanism analyses are the quantitative description of
the limitation, not independent stories.
sections.text: Four controlled experiments pin down where the amplification lives and how much overlap it takes to trigger it: a three-source decomposition localises the amplification to the learned policy — the ODE solver contributes exactly zero at the boundary from 25 25 to 400 400 steps, KL-anchor mismatch is bounded and moves the boundary non-systematically, and the residual 15 15 – 78 % 78\% shortfall is policy-side (Appendix F ); saddle-corridor routing is separately rejected, so the limitation is a static representational shortfall, not trajectory re-routing (Section 5.1, Appendix E ); the α ⁡ ( g ) = β c / β cross \alpha(g)=\beta_{c}/\beta_{\rm cross} scan quantifies how deep into overlap the geometry must fall before the limitation bites (Appendix I ); and the bidirectional reachability test shows that the tight GMM geometry is unattainable from the Gaussian ELBO, closing the loop on why the prior — not its hyperparameters — must change (Appendices G , K ). The paper’s causal chain is therefore prior type ⟹ ELBO ⇒ d min / ( 2 ​ σ 0 ) ⟹ policy-side amplification ⟹ β c ​ and coverage plateau , \boxed{\text{prior type}}\Longrightarrow\boxed{\text{ELBO }\Rightarrow\;d_{\min}/(2\sigma_{0})}\Longrightarrow\boxed{\text{policy-side amplification}}\Longrightarrow\boxed{\beta_{c}\text{ and coverage plateau}}, (causal-chain) and the core conclusion is conditional rather than comparative: not “a mixture prior is better than a Gaussian”, but when the latent geometry would fall into the overlap regime, a non-Gaussian prior is necessary, because it preserves mode separation and thereby sidesteps the error amplification of the current pipeline . The remainder develops the variational theory and its crossover scale (§4), the experiments and the three-source decomposition (§5), and supporting appendices: the four-prior family comparison ( H ), fixed-prior and matched-geometry interventions ( G , K ), separation and rare-basin scans ( I , J ), and the machine-checked theory skeleton ( L ).

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: This work intersects four active research threads.

sections.heading: 2.1 VAE prior choice and downstream impact
sections.text: The standard VAE uses a Gaussian prior ( Kingma and Welling, 2013 ) , but numerous alternatives have been proposed to better capture multi-modal data. Jiang et al. (2017) introduced VaDE, which replaces the Gaussian prior with a GMM and shows improvements in clustering quality. Tomczak and Welling (2018) proposed VampPriors (learnable mixture priors parameterised by a decoder network), and Lee et al. (2021) introduced GMVAE, which combines a GMM prior with a structured inference network. These works all report that richer priors improve disentanglement and reconstruction quality, but none has studied the interaction between prior width and the critical RL fine-tune boundary that is our focus. The posterior-collapse literature ( Bowman et al., 2016 ; Alemi et al., 2018 ) diagnosed how a Gaussian prior lets the aggregated posterior match it by construction ( Hoffman and Johnson, 2016 ; Moyer et al., 2018 ) ; on real multimodal structure data the mismatch is concrete — cryo-EM heterogeneous reconstruction with Gaussian-prior VAEs shows the aggregate posterior spilling past the prior’s support ( Zhong et al., 2021 ) . Propositions 2 and 3 give that intuition its quantitative, boundary-facing form — the KL term actively taxes separation and tightness rather than merely ignoring them — and connect it to β c \beta_{c} rather than to base-model quality.

sections.heading: 2.2 Latent diffusion models
sections.text: The stable-diffusion family ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) demonstrated that VAE priors are practically interchangeable with a Gaussian, and most subsequent work on latent diffusion ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Kingma and Dhariwal, 2021 ) continues to use Gaussian priors by default. The recipe is deployed infrastructure rather than a toy setting — latent video diffusion scales it to large video corpora ( Blattmann et al., 2023 ) , and diffusion-based design tools inherit the same generative stack for scientific applications ( Watson et al., 2023 ) — so a design choice inside the latent space has practical consequences. Our work shows that prior choice matters dramatically for fine-tuning robustness , even if it matters little for base-model quality.

sections.heading: 2.3 RL fine-tuning of generative models
sections.text: RLHF ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ) and DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) have become standard tools for aligning large language models, and the recipe is now spreading to diffusion: DDPO ( Black et al., 2024 ) treats denoising as an MDP for policy-gradient reward maximisation, DPOK ( Wallace et al., 2023 ) identifies the KL anchor as the key stabiliser, and text-to-image alignment studies report the resulting diversity loss ( Lee et al., 2023 ) . These observations belong to the reward-side regime: diversity erodes because the reward is pursued too far past its design envelope, the classical over-optimisation scaling of Gao et al. (2023) . Our subject is a different, upstream regime: even with a well-designed reward and a generous KL anchor, the collapse boundary is set by the prior’s geometry — the two failure modes are complementary, not competing, and neither subsumes the other. Poole et al. (2022) introduced stochastic gradient methods for diffusion fine-tuning with KL anchors, and Dhariwal et al. (2023) showed that reward-weighted diffusion produces mode collapse at sufficiently large β \beta . Lu et al. (2024) identified a phase transition in reverse-KL fine-tuning and called for theoretical understanding of the critical β c \beta_{c} — our work answers this call by connecting β c \beta_{c} to prior geometry.

sections.heading: 3 Theory
sections.text: We now connect the experimental findings to a closed-form analysis of reverse-KL RL fine-tuning. The key insight is that prior geometry — specifically the VAE’s latent-space mode width σ lat \sigma_{\mathrm{lat}} — is the first-order determinant of the critical β c \beta_{c} below which the model collapses toward the RL target.

sections.heading: 3.6 What the crossover-scale predictor actually predicts
sections.text: The above analysis refines our interpretation of β cross \beta_{\mathrm{cross}} . It correctly predicts that σ Gauss > σ GMM \sigma_{\mathrm{Gauss}}>\sigma_{\mathrm{GMM}} implies β c Gauss > β c GMM \beta_{c}^{\mathrm{Gauss}}>\beta_{c}^{\mathrm{GMM}} (Proposition 1, monotonicity), but it does not predict the magnitude of the gap, because the dominant contribution comes from the dynamic error amplification ratio, not the variational ratio. sections.heading: 3.7 Variational vs. dynamic: the 50 × 50\times systematic gap
sections.text: The variational analysis above gives the exact reverse-KL optimum π ∗ \pi^{*} . Our RL fine-tune uses score matching + ODE sampling from a learned diffusion model, which approximates π ∗ \pi^{*} with three putative sources of systematic error: (1) policy-network approximation and optimisation (the 2-layer MLP score represents the tilted gradient field imperfectly, and 1000 1000 guidance steps need not reach the reverse-KL optimum); (2) ODE discretisation of the PF-ODE; (3) KL-anchor mismatch (the reference is a diffusion model trained on the VAE’s aggregate posterior, not the exact GMM p 0 p_{0} ). Solver (source 2): zero at the boundary. The measured β c \beta_{c} is exactly invariant to step count N ∈ [ 25,400 ] N\in[25,400] ( 0.0 % 0.0\% shift) for every geometry. sections.text: The variational bound (and Proposition 4 ) assume separated modes: d min > 4 ​ σ 0 d_{\min}>4\sigma_{0} , so that the 2 σ 0 \sigma_{0} Gaussian balls do not overlap at β = 0 \beta=0 . sections.heading: Why does dyn / var \mathrm{dyn}/\mathrm{var} exist?
sections.text: The small but systematic dyn / var ≈ 2 × \mathrm{dyn}/\mathrm{var}\approx 2\times even in well-separated regimes is consistent with score-network approximation error near mode saddle points, where the tilted-GMM gradient varies most sharply (Fig. 5 ). Whether saddle error also explains the much larger gaps under compression is not established by the regional data: Appendix D shows that the raw grid MSE at saddles is largest for narrow , well-separated modes (up to 603 × 603\times the mode MSE) and falls to ≈ 1 × \approx 1\times when modes broaden and overlap, while the density-weighted MSE stays close to the mode MSE in every configuration — saddle-grid errors by themselves carry essentially no stationary mass. The 80 × 80\times gap in Exp7’s Gaussian-prior runs therefore cannot be attributed to saddle MSE on overlap grounds alone. A natural hypothesis is that fine-tuning changes where the controlled trajectories travel, so that they cross saddle corridors where the reference score is wrong and a grid-localised error becomes a boundary shift. We tested this corridor-routing mechanism directly by evaluating score error along controlled PF-ODE trajectories (next paragraph; Appendix E ): across 24 GMM geometries, collapsing fine-tunes do not spend more time in saddle strips and the reference-score error encountered along their paths stays near the reference-path value for the median configuration. Corridor routing is therefore not the carrier of β c dyn \beta_{c}^{\mathrm{dyn}} : the follow-up budget decomposition (Appendix F ) identifies it instead as a static policy-side gap — finite-capacity representation of the tilted score field and/or incomplete reverse-KL optimisation — with zero solver contribution and a bounded, non-systematic anchor contribution. Neither equals the push-forward measure of the PF-ODE driven by the fine-tuned score at finite β \beta , which is the measure that actually decides whether controlled trajectories reach the target. sections.heading: 4.3 Exp5A: prior comparison in a controlled 1D setting
sections.text: We begin with the simplest experiment that directly isolates the prior effect: a 1D target distribution with K = 10 K=10 Gaussian modes packed in a d = 5 d=5 interval, compared under two VAE priors — a standard Gaussian and a mixture-of-Gaussians fitted to the target mode structure. The target is intentionally chosen to be simple (1D, well-separated modes) so that the prior effect is not confounded by VAE latent geometry distortions.

sections.heading: Two observations from one experiment.
sections.text: Exp5A gives two results simultaneously: 1. The collapse position is identical for both priors. Both the Gaussian and GMM priors show β c = 100 \beta_{c}=100 (log-interpolated, coverage first reaches 0.5 0.5 ) — the collapse boundary is prior-independent, as the variational theory predicts. Neither prior is therefore more collapse- resistant in this controlled setting: the onset of collapse happens at the same regularisation strength. This directly validates Main Line 1. 2. But the collapse plateau depends strongly on the prior. At β = 10000 \beta=10000 (deep in the non-collapse regime), the GMM prior recovers 100 % 100\% of target modes, while the Gaussian prior plateaus at 70 % 70\% coverage. The GMM prior preserves three additional modes that the Gaussian prior permanently loses, even at arbitrarily large β \beta . This directly validates Main Line 2. The collapse boundary — where coverage transitions from near-zero to near-plateau — depends only on the latent geometry, not on whether the prior is unimodal or multi-modal. But the plateau ceiling — how many modes are ultimately recoverable — is entirely determined by the prior. Fig. 6 shows both effects simultaneously. The subsequent experiments (Exp6, Exp7) test these two lines in progressively more complex settings, and show how the bridging mechanism (dyn/var) modulates them. sections.heading: 4.4 Exp6: crowded latent space (K=30)
sections.text: We first test our mechanism in a controlled toy setting: 30 modes packed into a d = 8 d=8 Gaussian arrangement ( lattice_pack construction), compressed into a 2D VAE latent. The large mode count ensures the latent space is crowded — a priori the worst case for mode preservation. We compare two VAE configurations, each in 3 independent random seeds: • Gaussian prior 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) : the standard VAE default. • GMM prior (VaDE-style EMA target, Gaussian KL warmup 3k steps): a mixture of 30 unit-width Gaussians whose means follow the same lattice-pack layout. Each seed pipeline: VAE 30k steps, score diffusion 40k steps on the aggregate posterior, then reverse-KL RL fine-tune at 12 β \beta values { 0.1 , 0.5 , 1 , 5 , 10 , 50 , 100 , 500 , 1000 , 2000 , 5000 , 10000 } \{0.1,0.5,1,5,10,50,100,500,1000,2000,5000,10000\} , F ​ T = 1000 FT=1000 steps each, λ = 1.0 \lambda=1.0 . Coverage is evaluated by mode_masses (2 σ 0 \sigma_{0} radius, nearest-neighbour assignment) on 8000 ODE samples at 150 Euler steps.

sections.heading: Why the latent β c \beta_{c} is less separated.
sections.text: The latent β c \beta_{c} shows a smaller mean gap of 1.22 × 1.22\times (sd 0.38), with one seed (seed 2) actually showing GMM slightly larger ( 1.90 1.90 vs. 1.55 1.55 ). This is expected: the latent-space β c \beta_{c} is a weaker bound than the decoded one — a diffusion model can land its modes near the correct latent means ( cov lat ≈ 1 \mathrm{cov}_{\mathrm{lat}}\approx 1 ) while the decoder still scrambles their identities ( cov dec < 1 \mathrm{cov}_{\mathrm{dec}}<1 ). In the two-stage reading of the Gaussian limitation, these are its two consecutive consequences: the prior compresses the latent geometry first (latent β c \beta_{c} rises — the 1.22 × 1.22\times gap), and the decoder, trained on already-overlapped latents, loses mode identity independently of where fine-tuning later lands (the decoded plateau ceiling cov dec ≈ 0.63 \mathrm{cov}_{\mathrm{dec}}\approx 0.63 under the Gaussian prior that no β \beta recovers). The decoded metric is thus the latent compression after amplification by the decoder — a bounded 1.22 × 1.22\times latent gap becomes a 3.83 × 3.83\times decoded gap plus a plateau loss, because the non-injective decoder turns reduced latent separation into lost mode identity; the theory (§ 3 ) explains why the latent β c \beta_{c} can be non-monotone with σ lat \sigma_{\mathrm{lat}} in crowded geometries. sections.heading: 4.5 Exp7: real molecular dataset (alanine-dipeptide)
sections.text: Exp7 moves beyond synthetic toy data to a real molecular conformational dataset. We run a 20 ns Langevin MD trajectory on alanine-dipeptide (ACE-ALA-NME) with OBC2 implicit solvent at 300 K ( alanine_data.py ), extract the 45 heavy-atom pair distances, and whitened-PCA down to 10 dimensions. Backbone ( ϕ , ψ ) (\phi,\psi) torsions label 3 physical basins via TorusKDE2D: Basin Frequency Occupancy C7eq 0.435 dominant alpha_R 0.338 secondary beta/C5 0.157 rarest C7ax and alpha_L are never visited in 20 ns (0 frames, 95% CI excludes both from the 3 active basins). We run the same two-VAE pipeline in 3 seeds, with one key difference: the RL reward target z t z_{t} is the rarest basin (beta/C5, 15.7% occupancy). This is the hardest test case: an RL agent that collapses toward the common modes loses the already-rare one entirely.

sections.text: The two experiments — synthetic crowded toy (K=30, 8D data → \to 2D latent) and real molecular dataset (3 conformational basins, 45 distances → \to PCA (10) → \to 2D latent) — agree on the qualitative pattern: 1. sections.heading: Soft coverage: a fine-grained view of the collapse transition.
sections.text: Figure 10 and Table 7 compare hard and soft coverage curves for both priors. The hard ball-coverage metric assigns each sample to exactly one mode (nearest centre within radius 2 ​ σ 0 2\sigma_{0} ; metrics.mode_masses ) and then declares a mode “recovered” when its assigned mass exceeds 0.5 / K 0.5/K . In the overlap regime this produces two pathologies: (i) a mode that has lost most of its mass but still lies inside the 2 ​ σ 0 2\sigma_{0} ball is counted as fully recovered; (ii) a mode that has narrowly escaped the ball is counted as fully lost. The metric can therefore jump discretely between 1 / K 1/K , 2 / K 2/K , … \ldots , and its collapse boundary depends on the ball radius rather than on the actual mass distribution. To obtain a continuous, radius-free diagnostic we re-ran Exp7 seed 0 with a Gaussian-kernel soft mass, m k soft = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N 𝒩 ⁡ ( z i , μ k , σ 0 2 ​ I ) ∑ j = 1 K 𝒩 ⁡ ( z i , μ j , σ 0 2 ​ I ) , cov soft = ∑ k = 1 K min ⁡ ( m k soft w k , 1 ) ​ w k ∑ j w j , m_{k}^{\mathrm{soft}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{\mathcal{N}(z_{i};\,\mu_{k},\sigma_{0}^{2}I)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\mathcal{N}(z_{i};\,\mu_{j},\sigma_{0}^{2}I)},\qquad\mathrm{cov}_{\mathrm{soft}}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\min\!\left(\frac{m_{k}^{\mathrm{soft}}}{w_{k}},1\right)\frac{w_{k}}{\sum_{j}w_{j}}, (2) which assigns each sample fractionally to every mode (rows of the N × K N\times K weight matrix sum to 1 1 ) and weights mode recovery by the target basin frequencies w k w_{k} . Unlike hard coverage, cov soft \mathrm{cov}_{\mathrm{soft}} never saturates: a tilted distribution that concentrates near a single mode approaches, but does not reach, zero for the other modes. Gaussian prior ( d min / σ 0 = 1.61 d_{\min}/\sigma_{0}=1.61 , overlap). The soft and hard curves tell the same qualitative story but reveal different fine structure. At the lowest scan point β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 , the hard metric reports cov hard = 0.33 \mathrm{cov}_{\mathrm{hard}}=0.33 (only one of three modes inside the ball), while the soft metric reports cov soft = 0.56 \mathrm{cov}_{\mathrm{soft}}=0.56 : the two “lost” modes still carry ∼ 23 % \sim 23\% of residual soft mass that the hard ball discards. At β = 0.5 \beta=0.5 – 1 1 , both metrics sit near 0.65 0.65 – 0.72 0.72 . Above β = 5 \beta=5 , the hard metric saturates at 1.00 1.00 for all remaining β \beta values, whereas the soft metric continues to rise smoothly from 0.85 0.85 ( β = 5 \beta=5 ) to 0.95 0.95 ( β ≥ 500 \beta\geq 500 ), showing that the high- β \beta “full recovery” is only asymptotically approached, not achieved. The hard β c \beta_{c} (log-interpolated at the 0.5 0.5 threshold) is 0.224 0.224 ; the soft β c \beta_{c} lies below the scan floor ( < 0.1 <0.1 ), because the fractional mass keeps the soft metric above threshold even when only one hard-ball mode is occupied. The two curves are strongly correlated (Pearson r = 0.96 r=0.96 ). GMM prior ( d min / σ 0 = 2.06 d_{\min}/\sigma_{0}=2.06 , separated). Here the two metrics agree on the qualitative conclusion but differ in their baseline . Hard coverage is 1.00 1.00 at every scan point from β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 upward: no collapse occurs within the scanned range (the bisect run in § 4.5 locates the true boundary at β c = 3.16 × 10 − 3 \beta_{c}=3.16\times 10^{-3} ). Soft coverage starts at 0.85 0.85 ( β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 ) and rises to a stable plateau of 0.94 0.94 for β ≥ 0.5 \beta\geq 0.5 , where it remains across four decades of β \beta with no collapse transition. The ≈ 0.06 \approx 0.06 gap between hard and soft plateau is systematic, not a sign of mode loss: even a perfectly mode- separated generated distribution has finite Gaussian-kernel overlap with neighbouring centres when σ 0 \sigma_{0} is the same bandwidth used for both the target and the assignment. What the soft metric adds. Three conclusions are specific to the soft view and are invisible to hard coverage. sections.heading: 5 Discussion and Open Problems
sections.text: The narrative of this paper is limitation → \to condition → \to remedy : the Gaussian prior’s structural limitation under RL fine-tuning (it packs multimodal data into an overlapping latent), the geometric condition under which the limitation bites ( d min / ( 2 ​ σ 0 ) < 1 d_{\min}/(2\sigma_{0})<1 ), and the remedy (a mode-preserving prior, necessary precisely in the overlap regime). The causal chain ( causal-chain ) that carries this narrative is supported by closed-form theory (Theorem 1 ), Exp5A/Exp6/Exp7 with ≥ 3 \geq 3 seeds each, controlled interventions that move geometry at a fixed prior and switch the prior at fixed geometry (Appendices G , K ), and cross-MD robustness (20 ns vs. 60 ns give identical β c \beta_{c} for matched priors). The mechanism material below — the dyn / var \mathrm{dyn}/\mathrm{var} decomposition, the corridor exclusion, and the α ⁡ ( g ) \alpha(g) scaling — is the quantitative description of the limitation , collected as supporting results: where the amplification lives (policy side), what it is not (solver, anchor, saddle routing), and how deep the overlap must be before it fires. We fix terminology, state the boundary condition on the remedy, give three implications, and end with the genuinely open question.

sections.heading: Terminology: collapse position versus coverage plateau.
sections.text: “Resistance to collapse” is ambiguous unless the two coordinates of the β \beta –coverage curve are kept separate. The position β c \beta_{c} (coverage first reaches 0.5 0.5 ) is prior-independent in well-separated geometry (Exp5A: both priors β c = 100 \beta_{c}{=}100 ; Exp6: 1.23 × 1.23\times apart). The unconditional multi-modal advantage is the plateau — modes still recoverable at β ≫ β c \beta\gg\beta_{c} ( 1.00 1.00 vs. 0.70 0.70 in Exp5A; 0.73 0.73 vs. 0.58 0.58 decoded in Exp6). The Exp7 position gap ( 0.224 0.224 vs. 3.16 × 10 − 3 3.16\times 10^{-3} ) is no exception: it appears only because the two priors induce different geometries ( d min / ( 2 ​ σ 0 ) = 0.81 d_{\min}/(2\sigma_{0})=0.81 vs. 1.03 1.03 ), vanishes in seed 2 where the Gaussian geometry also overlaps ( 0.99 0.99 , gap ≤ 1.4 × \leq 1.4\times ), and is thus the indirect chain prior → \to ELBO → \to geometry → \to amplification → \to β c \beta_{c} , not a direct prior effect. Below, “lower β c \beta_{c} ” names the position and “higher recovery” the plateau.

sections.heading: Boundary condition on the remedy.
sections.text: The two benefits have different limits, and stating both is what keeps the claim from reading as “GMM always wins”. (i) The position gap is a finite-resource effect: its carrier is policy-side error under overlap (zero solver contribution, bounded anchor; Appendix F ), so a sufficiently expressive, fully optimised policy should drive β c dyn / β c var → 1 \beta_{c}^{\rm dyn}/\beta_{c}^{\rm var}\to 1 and close the position gap toward the variational order-1 prediction ( 0.69 × 0.69\times in Exp7) at fixed geometry. Policy capacity/budget scaling is the direct falsification experiment. (ii) The plateau gap lives one stage earlier, in the VAE representation itself: strong KL pressure on a Gaussian prior removes modes at the decoder even before RL fine-tuning (the w kl = 3 w_{\rm kl}{=}3 cell of Appendix G decodes only 0.90 0.90 of modes pre-fine-tuning at latent coverage 1.0 1.0 , and its post-fine-tuning plateau is 0.80 0.80 ), so the plateau advantage does not vanish with a larger RL policy — it requires changing the prior or the VAE objective. What is unconditional is therefore the plateau; what is finite-resource is the position gap. A cleaner reverse-KL solver or deeper policy could erase (i)’s amplification-driven component without touching (ii).

sections.heading: Implication 1: the advantage is geometric, not symbolic.
sections.text: The benefit is not the mixture symbol but the ELBO’s preservation of the data’s mode separation; any prior producing that geometry should behave likewise, so the GMM is one representative of a broader class of mode-separating priors ( Tomczak and Welling, 2018 ; Lee et al., 2021 ) . The four-prior comparison (Appendix H ) supports the conditional statement (emp/var within 0.43 0.43 – 1.24 1.24 of each cell’s own-geometry variational boundary across Gaussian, GMM, VampPrior and GMVAE, all plateaus full) while showing the symbol is not sufficient under the same budget: the label-free mixtures do not reach the tight GMM geometry (VampPrior d min / ( 2 ​ σ ) = 1.7 d_{\min}/(2\sigma)=1.7 , GMVAE 1.1 1.1 with components 0.67 ​ d 0.67d off-mode). The remaining item is the ELBO recipe that gets a label-free mixture there, not the conditional claim.

the magnitude.
sections.text: Theorem 1 predicts the sign of the small matched-width boundary difference, and in well-separated geometry the two boundaries coincide to resolution (Exp5A: identical; Exp6: 1.23 × 1.23\times ); the large overlap-regime magnitudes ( 71 × 71\times Exp7, 3 3 – 6 × 6\times Exp6) are policy-side amplification against an order-1 variational prediction ( 0.69 × 0.69\times ). The framework is thus a qualitative position guide that is silent about the plateau, with quantitative magnitudes requiring the mechanism below.

sections.heading: Open Problem 2 (resolved). The sources of dynamic amplification.
sections.text: The dyn / var \mathrm{dyn}/\mathrm{var} ratio conflates three error sources: policy-network approximation and optimisation, ODE discretisation, and KL anchor mismatch. Appendix F isolates all three on eight geometries: the solver contributes exactly zero at the boundary, anchor mismatch is bounded and moves the boundary non-systematically, and the residual 15 15 – 78 % 78\% is policy-side. sections.heading: Outlook: Applications to molecular generative models
sections.text: The mechanism we identify — that multi-modal priors preserve latent mode separation under ELBO training, raising the coverage plateau and, in overlap-prone geometries only, lowering the empirical collapse boundary — has direct implications for molecular generative models trained on equilibrium (Boltzmann) distributions. Standard diffusion training on molecular trajectories does not reweight by Boltzmann factors, so rare conformations are underrepresented; QBM-VAE ( Noé et al., 2021 ; Ding et al., 2023 ) and related methods use VAE encoders to define collective variables for enhanced sampling. Exp7 established the geometry on alanine-dipeptide’s three conformational basins, and Experiment X (Appendix J ) now runs the dedicated rare-basin reward test on the same real MD trajectory: directing a reverse-KL reward at the rare C5 basin ( w = 0.157 w=0.157 ), Gaussian-prior guidance reaches ≈ 4 × \approx 4\times enrichment but erases one of the two common basins, whereas the tight label-tracked GMM reaches 2.9 2.9 – 3.6 × 3.6\times while retaining every common basin above threshold (3 seeds). The causal chain ( causal-chain ) thus extends to physical conformations in a refined form: prior geometry chooses a point on the enrichment–retention Pareto frontier — sharp control with destruction versus softer, basin-preserving enrichment, the latter mediated by the decoder’s amplification of a diffuse latent “collapse”. Two caveats bound the application claim: the preserving mechanism relies on the small 2D-latent decoder being non-injective on the GMM’s tight components, and 3 × 3\times enrichment is physically unreachable for the two common basins ( 1 / w ≤ 3 1/w\leq 3 ) for either prior. The ongoing 100 ns MD experiment, which may produce K ≥ 5 K\geq 5 physical basins, together with higher-capacity decoders and additional small molecules, is the natural next test of whether the j 2 j^{2} K K -scaling of Appendix I and the Pareto trade-off of Appendix J survive realistic settings.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: The Gaussian prior’s failure under RL fine-tuning is geometric. Its ELBO optimum compresses multimodal data into an overlapping latent, and KL-anchored fine-tuning amplifies that overlap into a collapse boundary far above the variational scale. The separation-to-width ratio is the single mediator of this effect: it is moved by the prior and by nothing else we could isolate. The claim is conditional. A non-Gaussian prior is necessary precisely when the latent geometry would otherwise fall into the overlap regime and the downstream task is coverage-sensitive; outside that regime the Gaussian default suffices. Within it, two gaps must be kept apart: the boundary position is a finite-resource pipeline effect, while the coverage plateau is a representational property of the VAE itself. The practical upshot is that prior choice is a geometric lever that can be checked before training, and the conceptual upshot is that the KL term does not merely ignore mode structure — it prices it.

sections.heading: Appendix E Score error along controlled PF-ODE trajectories
sections.text: This appendix reports the direct test of the corridor-routing hypothesis discussed in Section 5.1: instead of evaluating the score error on a uniform grid or on reference p t p_{t} samples, we integrate the controlled PF-ODE and accumulate the reference-score error and the policy deviation along the trajectories themselves . Script: expP_paths.py ; aggregation: analyze_expP.py ; raw outputs: results/expP_paths/*.json .

sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: The 24 geometries are the 12-point 2D width sweep ( K ∈ { 5 , 10 , 20 } K\in\{5,10,20\} , σ ∈ { 0.25 , 0.5 , 1 , 2 } \sigma\in\{0.25,0.5,1,2\} , d = 5 d=5 ) and the 2D/3D lattice packs ( K ∈ { 5 , 10 , 20 } K\in\{5,10,20\} , d ∈ { 3 , 5 } d\in\{3,5\} , σ = 1 \sigma=1 ); 4D/5D packs are excluded because their reference checkpoints are not fully trained (Appendix D ). For each geometry we load the reference checkpoint and its empirical exact-grid β c \beta_{c} from results/expA_scale , then fine-tune three policies at β ∈ { 0.3 , 1 , 3 } ​ β c \beta\in\{0.3,1,3\}\,\beta_{c} with reverse-KL guidance, λ = 1 \lambda=1 , 1000 1000 steps, S = 20 S=20 , batch size 256 256 , learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , seed 0. All four models are integrated from the same batch of 4096 4096 terminal states x T x_{T} (fixed seed), so path divergence is attributable to the score functions alone. Integration uses the RK2 PF-ODE drift of diffusion.ode_sample bit-identically on the time grid linspace ⁡ ( 1 , 10 − 3 , 201 ) \mathrm{linspace}(1,10^{-3},201) , repeated at 480 480 steps as a discretisation control. At every intermediate state we evaluate ‖ s ^ ref − s ∗ ‖ 2 \|\hat{s}_{\rm ref}-s_{*}\|^{2} and ‖ s ^ π − s ∗ ‖ 2 \|\hat{s}_{\pi}-s_{*}\|^{2} against the analytic blurred target score dist.blurred_score , and classify the state into mode/saddle/valley with the exact region rules and thresholds of metrics.score_mse_nd ; region labels are recomputed at each state. sections.heading: Intentional tilt versus reference error.
sections.text: Along collapsing paths, the policy’s own deviation ‖ s ^ π − s ∗ ‖ 2 \|\hat{s}_{\pi}-s_{*}\|^{2} in saddle strips is 4 4 – 1,950 × 1{,}950\times the reference error (median 26 × 26\times over geometries), including broad-mode configurations whose reference scores are accurate (e.g. 326 × 326\times at K = 10 , σ = 2 K{=}10,\sigma{=}2 ). Collapse therefore tracks the imposed reward tilt rather than pre-existing regions of reference inaccuracy.

sections.heading: Verdict.
sections.text: The corridor hypothesis predicts that collapsing policies spend substantially more trajectory time in saddle strips and accumulate substantially larger path-weighted reference error. Residence is unchanged (median + 7 % +7\% ), the median error ratio is near unity in every time window, and the sole large amplification is a single narrow, few-mode geometry. Corridor routing is rejected as a general mechanism; it can survive only as a geometry-specific amplifier, and any Gaussian-prior latent version requires the analogous experiment in latent space, which the present data-space suite does not cover.

Two priors — Gaussian and the label-tracked GMM — are trained at the full budget (30 000 VAE steps, 40 000 score steps), three seeds each. For every target basin separately, the policy is fine-tuned (reverse KL, 1000 steps) on a 12-point β \beta grid anchored at max ⁡ ( β c var , 2 ​ σ lat 2 ) \max(\beta_{c}^{\rm var},2\sigma_{\rm lat}^{2}) , and N = 8000 N=8000 ODE samples are measured in four spaces: latent/decoded × \times hard/soft. Enrichment is m t / w t m_{t}/w_{t} ; hard retention is the fraction of non-target basins still holding mass ≥ 0.5 / K \geq 0.5/K ; soft retention is the weight-capped recovery fraction. Soft kernels use σ = d min / 2 \sigma=d_{\min}/2 in each space (latent ≈ 0.027 \approx 0.027 , decoded ≈ 0.98 \approx 0.98 ): the fitted diagnostic width σ x ≈ 2.87 \sigma_{x}\approx 2.87 exceeds the basin spacing and flattens kernel weights, whereas d min / 2 d_{\min}/2 keeps adjacent basins distinguishable.

sections.heading: Accounting caveat: the soft metric at fixed enrichment.
sections.text: Soft kernel masses sum to one, so soft retention at a fixed enrichment E E is pinned by mass conservation, ( 1 − E ​ w t ) / ∑ k ≠ t w k (1-Ew_{t})/\sum_{k\neq t}w_{k} : for C5 at E = 3 E=3 this is 0.684 0.684 , and all six cells return 0.684 0.684 to three decimals. We report soft curves and AUCs, but the discrimination between priors at fixed enrichment comes from the hard gate, which is not mass-conservation constrained.

Result 1: 3 × 3\times enrichment is physically reachable only
for the rare basin.
sections.text: Maximum hard decoded enrichment for the two common basins is bounded by 1 / w 1/w : 2.3 2.3 ( β \beta ) and 3.0 3.0 ( α R \alpha_{R} ). Observed maxima are 2.2 2.2 and 2.4 2.4 (Gaussian) and 1.3 1.3 and 1.7 1.7 (GMM), so no common basin crosses 3 × 3\times for either prior; these cells are censored above rather than extrapolated. C5 admits 1 / w ≈ 6.4 1/w\approx 6.4 and is the discriminating target.

sections.heading:
Result 2: on C5, Gaussian guidance is sharp but destructive;
GMM guidance is soft and preserving.
sections.text: Gaussian-prior policies reach 3.9 3.9 – 4.3 × 4.3\times hard enrichment of C5 in all three seeds, but hard retention is 0.5 0.5 everywhere at 3 × 3\times : exactly one of the two other basins falls below 0.5 / K 0.5/K . GMM-prior policies reach 3.5 3.5 – 3.6 × 3.6\times with hard retention 1.0 1.0 in two seeds; the third peaks at 2.91 × 2.91\times (censored below 3 × 3\times ) with retention 1.0 1.0 across the entire sweep (Figure 24 ). Soft AUCs favour or match the GMM on every basin ( 0.97 0.97 vs 0.80 0.80 on β \beta ; comparable on α R \alpha_{R} and C5), and the full Pareto curves (Figure 23 ) show the GMM trading enrichment for retention strictly less steeply once the hard gate begins to bind.

sections.heading:
Result 3: mechanism — diffuse latent “collapse” plus
decoder amplification.
sections.text: The GMM latent is tight ( σ lat = 0.027 \sigma_{\rm lat}=0.027 – 0.030 0.030 , d min / ( 2 ​ σ lat ) ≈ 0.9 d_{\min}/(2\sigma_{\rm lat})\approx 0.9 – 1.0 1.0 ; component centres only 0.055 0.055 apart). At the smallest β \beta , hard latent target mass reaches only ≈ 0.22 \approx 0.22 : the f = 0.5 f=0.5 coverage criterion is met (the other balls hold < 0.5 / K <0.5/K each) but 78 % 78\% of samples lie in the inter-ball tail, and the deterministic decoder, with a gain of ≈ 36 \approx 36 from latent to feature spacing ( 1.96 / 0.055 1.96/0.055 ), spreads that tail back across all three physical basins. The Exp7 coverage sweep shows the same signature directly: latent coverage stays at 1 / 3 1/3 from β = 10 − 6 \beta=10^{-6} to 2 × 10 − 3 2\times 10^{-3} while decoded coverage stays at 1.0 1.0 . Gaussian-prior collapse is instead sharp (latent target mass 0.91 0.91 ), and the decoder transmits it faithfully, which is what makes 4 × 4\times enrichment possible — and what erases a basin.

sections.heading: Verdict.
sections.text: On real molecular data the conditional causal chain survives in a more interesting form than “GMM is uniformly better”: the prior’s geometry selects a point on the enrichment–retention Pareto frontier. The Gaussian prior offers controllable, sharp rare-basin enrichment at the price of basin destruction; the tight GMM prior trades ≈ 20 % \approx 20\% of reachable enrichment for full retention of the common basins. Limits: 2D latent, K = 3 K=3 , and the preserving mechanism relies on the decoder’s non-injective amplification, which should be re-audited for higher-capacity decoders and larger molecules. sections.heading: Appendix K Reverse counterfactual: matched-geometry prior switch
sections.text: Appendix G fills the forward mediation cell: prior label fixed at Gaussian, geometry moved by the KL weight, and β c \beta_{c} follows geometry. Implication 2’s full-mediation claim is symmetric: at matched geometry, switching the prior label must not move β c \beta_{c} . sections.heading: Why the reverse cell needs a new intervention.
sections.text: One might expect the GMM analogue of expR — simply down-weighting the GMM KL term — to widen the encoder blobs and reproduce compressed geometries. It does not. The label-tracked GMM component means and variances EMA-track the encoder’s own per-label batch statistics ( 0.99 0.99 decay), so the GMM KL is self-referential: it contains neither the centre contraction toward the origin nor the width inflation toward unit variance that KL ( q ∥ 𝒩 ( 0 , I ) ) \mathrm{KL}(q\|\mathcal{N}(0,I)) imposes. Probe runs (30 000 VAE steps, seed 0) with the GMM KL weight spanning w kl ∈ { 0.003 , 0.01 , 0.03 , 0.1 , 0.3 , 1 , 3 } w_{\rm kl}\in\{0.003,0.01,0.03,0.1,0.3,1,3\} achieve g = d min / ( 2 ​ σ lat ) = 3.1 g=d_{\min}/(2\sigma_{\rm lat})=3.1 – 6.8 6.8 at every weight — never entering the Gaussian-ELBO image, whose widest geometry on this pack is g = 2.08 g=2.08 (the expR w kl = 0.03 w_{\rm kl}{=}0.03 cell). Reweighting therefore cannot produce the reverse counterfactual.

sections.heading: Verdict for Implication 2 (reverse cell).
sections.text: Within the reachable interior g ∈ [ 1.1 , 2.1 ] g\in[1.1,2.1] , geometry is a sufficient statistic for the collapse boundary across the prior switch: at matched geometry (with the absolute scale retained through β c var \beta_{c}^{\rm var} ), the measured boundaries agree to within the ± 25 % \pm 25\% CI, and any residual is the same finite-pipeline shortfall observed under both labels. The result does not extend to the two unreachable endpoints discussed next, where only one prior produces the geometry and no cross-label comparison exists.

sections.heading: Bidirectional reachability limit.

Both ends of the range remain single-prior observations and are reported as unreachable rather than synthesised: (i) the tight Exp6/V GMM endpoint g = 3.34 g=3.34 – 5.2 5.2 is not attained by any Gaussian-prior ELBO on this pack (image edge g ≈ 2.11 g\approx 2.11 ), and (ii) the compressed Gaussian tail ( g = 0.85 g=0.85 three-seed mean at w kl = 3 w_{\rm kl}{=}3 , reaching g ≈ 0.65 g\approx 0.65 in the expR seed-0 cell) is not attained by any GMM intervention probed: weight reweighting stays at g ≥ 3.1 g\geq 3.1 , width flooring bottoms out at g ≈ 2.04 g\approx 2.04 ( σ floor = 1.3 \sigma_{\rm floor}=1.3 ) because centre separation grows with component width, and centre contraction bottoms out at g ≈ 1.17 g\approx 1.17 ( α = 0.5 \alpha=0.5 ) as centres and widths contract together. Affiliation: Department of Chemical Engineering Affiliation: Tsinghua University Abstract Latent diffusion models almost universally place a Gaussian prior 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) on the VAE latent space. For base generation this default is unproblematic; under reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, however, it carries a structural limitation. We show that the standard VAE’s KL term does not merely ignore mode structure — it actively taxes separation and tightness. When the data are multimodal, the ELBO optimum therefore compresses distinct modes into an overlapping latent envelope. RL fine-tuning amplifies this overlap: the score network is under-resolved on the saddle region between modes, the dynamic-to-variational error amplification rises sharply, and the collapse boundary β c \beta_{c} — the minimum KL strength that preserves mode coverage — is pushed far above its variational scale. The effect is large and reproducible: on the real alanine-dipeptide Boltzmann distribution, a Gaussian-prior VAE collapses at β c = 0.224 \beta_{c}=0.224 , while a mode-tracked Gaussian-mixture prior on the same data collapses at 3.16 × 10 − 3 3.16\times 10^{-3} — a 71 × 71\times gap produced by the same pipeline. We trace this gap to a single geometric mediator, d min / ( 2 ​ σ 0 ) d_{\min}/(2\sigma_{0}) , and verify the causal chain through controlled interventions: moving geometry at fixed prior, and switching prior at matched geometry (full mediation; prior-label coefficient 0.995 × 0.995\times , 95% CI [ 0.79 , 1.25 ] [0.79,1.25] ). A three-source decomposition localises the amplification to the learned policy (zero ODE-solver contribution, bounded and non-systematic anchor mismatch); the coverage plateau, by contrast, is an unconditional benefit of mode-separating priors that no amount of RL capacity recovers. We state the remedy conditionally: a non-Gaussian prior is necessary precisely when the latent geometry would fall into the overlap regime and the downstream task is coverage-sensitive. A machine-checked theory skeleton (Lean 4) supports the KL pricing structure — a divergent compactness tax under a Gaussian prior versus a finite assignment fee under a mixture — and the position-versus-plateau distinction delimits what is finite-resource from what requires changing the prior. 1 Introduction Diffusion models are now the dominant paradigm in generative modelling: denoising diffusion probabilistic models ( Ho et al., 2020 ) and their score-based SDE generalisation ( Song et al., 2021 ) reach state-of-the-art sample quality through iterative denoising. Latent diffusion ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) made the paradigm scalable by running the diffusion process in the compressed latent space of a VAE ( Kingma and Welling, 2013 ) rather than in pixel space — the step that turned high-resolution and text-to-image synthesis into practical technology — and the latent-diffusion recipe now extends to video ( Blattmann et al., 2023 ) , while diffusion models more broadly have become standard tools in scientific design, from image scaffolds to de novo protein structure generation ( Watson et al., 2023 ) . In all of these deployed systems the VAE latent space carries a Gaussian prior 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) by default. A third layer is being installed on top of this stack: reinforcement-learning fine-tuning. DDPO ( Black et al., 2024 ) recasts denoising as a Markov decision process and maximises a downstream reward by policy gradient; DPOK ( Wallace et al., 2023 ) adds a KL regulariser anchoring the fine-tuned policy to the pretrained prior — the same alignment recipe that is mature on large language models ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) and is spreading rapidly across diffusion deployments. Latent diffusion pipelines thus almost universally place a Gaussian prior on the VAE latent space, and this default — unproblematic for base generation — carries a structural limitation that emerges precisely when the three layers above are combined: multimodal data, a tight VAE latent space, and RL fine-tuning. This paper asks when that limitation bites, why, and what to do about it. One clarification before the contribution: this is not yet another account of reward-overoptimisation. The RLHF literature already documents diversity loss from over-optimised rewards ( Gao et al., 2023 ; Lee et al., 2023 ) ; our concern is a different, upstream mechanism — the collapse boundary is set by prior geometry even when the reward is well designed and the KL strength is generous. Jiang et al. (2017) introduced VaDE, which replaces the Gaussian prior with a GMM and shows improvements in clustering quality. Tomczak and Welling (2018) proposed VampPriors (learnable mixture priors parameterised by a decoder network), and Lee et al. (2021) introduced GMVAE, which combines a GMM prior with a structured inference network. These works all report that richer priors improve disentanglement and reconstruction quality, but none has studied the interaction between prior width and the critical RL fine-tune boundary that is our focus. The posterior-collapse literature ( Bowman et al., 2016 ; Alemi et al., 2018 ) diagnosed how a Gaussian prior lets the aggregated posterior match it by construction ( Hoffman and Johnson, 2016 ; Moyer et al., 2018 ) ; on real multimodal structure data the mismatch is concrete — cryo-EM heterogeneous reconstruction with Gaussian-prior VAEs shows the aggregate posterior spilling past the prior’s support ( Zhong et al., 2021 ) . Propositions 2 and 3 give that intuition its quantitative, boundary-facing form — the KL term actively taxes separation and tightness rather than merely ignoring them — and connect it to β c \beta_{c} rather than to base-model quality. 2.2 Latent diffusion models The stable-diffusion family ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) demonstrated that VAE priors are practically interchangeable with a Gaussian, and most subsequent work on latent diffusion ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Kingma and Dhariwal, 2021 ) continues to use Gaussian priors by default. The recipe is deployed infrastructure rather than a toy setting — latent video diffusion scales it to large video corpora ( Blattmann et al., 2023 ) , and diffusion-based design tools inherit the same generative stack for scientific applications ( Watson et al., 2023 ) — so a design choice inside the latent space has practical consequences. Our work shows that prior choice matters dramatically for fine-tuning robustness , even if it matters little for base-model quality. 2.3 RL fine-tuning of generative models RLHF ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ) and DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) have become standard tools for aligning large language models, and the recipe is now spreading to diffusion: DDPO ( Black et al., 2024 ) treats denoising as an MDP for policy-gradient reward maximisation, DPOK ( Wallace et al., 2023 ) identifies the KL anchor as the key stabiliser, and text-to-image alignment studies report the resulting diversity loss ( Lee et al., 2023 ) . These observations belong to the reward-side regime: diversity erodes because the reward is pursued too far past its design envelope, the classical over-optimisation scaling of Gao et al. (2023) . Our subject is a different, upstream regime: even with a well-designed reward and a generous KL anchor, the collapse boundary is set by the prior’s geometry — the two failure modes are complementary, not competing, and neither subsumes the other. Poole et al. (2022) introduced stochastic gradient methods for diffusion fine-tuning with KL anchors, and Dhariwal et al.
